exercises.prompt: Write `git_blob_hash(data)`, which takes the contents of a file as `bytes` and returns the 40-character hexadecimal name Git gives it as a blob: the SHA-1 of the header `blob <size>`, a zero byte, and the contents. Check: `git_blob_hash(b"hello world\n")` is `3b18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad`.
exercises.starter:
import hashlib

def git_blob_hash(data):
    return hashlib.sha1(data).hexdigest()     # not yet: Git hashes a header too


print(git_blob_hash(b"hello world\n"))
exercises.tests:
assert git_blob_hash(b"hello world
") == "3b18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad", git_blob_hash(b"hello world
")
assert git_blob_hash(b"") == "e69de29bb2d1d6434b8b29ae775ad8c2e48c5391"
assert git_blob_hash("# Weather station
".encode()) == "439065236ff325d4a048bb041a7f1b9164d0c54f"
assert git_blob_hash("Kraków
".encode()) != git_blob_hash("Krakow
".encode())
hints: The header is the ASCII text `blob`, a space, the length of the contents in bytes as decimal digits, and a zero byte: `b"\0"`.
`len(data)` must count *bytes*, which it does because `data` is a `bytes` object. (For text, a character such as `ó` is two bytes in UTF-8.)

exercises.prompt: A repository's latest commit contains `README.md`, `docs/guide.md` and `src/station/sensors.py`, so its root tree has entries `README.md`, `docs` and `src`, and `src` contains the directory `station`. You edit **only** `src/station/sensors.py` and commit. How many new objects does Git create for this commit?

feedback.message: Not yet — you have counted the blob and the commit. Which trees list `sensors.py`, directly or through a subdirectory?
Not yet — count the trees on the path from the root to the changed file: there are three.
Not yet — you need more than one tree: a tree's hash changes whenever one of its entries changes.

hints: The changed file needs a new blob.
A tree's contents include the hashes of its entries. If a child's hash changes, the parent tree changes too, all the way up to the root.
Unchanged directories (`docs`) and files (`README.md`, `docs/guide.md`) are reused.

exercises.prompt: After `git rebase main`, every commit on your feature branch has a new hash, even though the changes in each commit look the same. Why?

options.label: Each replayed commit has a different parent (and usually a different tree), and both are part of the bytes that are hashed.
options.feedback: Yes. A commit's contents include `parent <hash>` and `tree <hash>`. Change the parent and the commit is a different object. The change ripples down the branch, since each later commit names the new hash of the one before.

options.label: Rebase adds a random value to each commit so that the old and new versions can be told apart.
options.feedback: Not yet — Git's objects are deterministic: the same contents always give the same hash. Nothing random is added.

options.label: Rebase recompresses the objects, and the hash is computed over the compressed bytes.
options.feedback: Not yet — the hash covers the uncompressed header and contents. Compression does not affect an object's name.

options.label: Commit hashes include the name of the branch the commit was made on.
options.feedback: Not yet — commits do not record branch names at all. A branch is just a ref pointing at a commit.

hints: Look at the output of `store.get(c2)` in the lesson: which lines would differ for a replayed commit?
exercises.solution: A commit object's bytes include its root tree hash, its parent hashes, the author and committer lines (with timestamps) and the message. Rebasing replays your changes onto a different base commit, so each replayed commit has a different `parent` line, usually a different tree (it now also contains `main`'s newer changes), and a new committer timestamp. Different bytes, different hash. Since the next commit names this new hash as *its* parent, every commit on the branch changes. This is exactly why rebasing commits that others have built on causes trouble: their history refers to the old hashes, which are no longer on your branch.

exercises.prompt: A commit graph is given as a dictionary `parents` mapping each commit id to the list of its parents. Write `merge_base(parents, a, b)`, which returns the **best common ancestor** of commits `a` and `b`: a commit that is an ancestor of both (a commit counts as its own ancestor) and is not an ancestor of any *other* common ancestor. The tests only use graphs where this commit is unique.
exercises.starter:
def merge_base(parents, a, b):
    return None


#     A - B - C - F        main
#          \     /
#           D - E          feature, merged into main at F
#                \
#                 G        more feature work
parents = {"A": [], "B": ["A"], "C": ["B"], "D": ["B"], "E": ["D"], "F": ["C", "E"], "G": ["E"]}
print(merge_base(parents, "F", "G"))    # E: the last feature commit that main has merged
exercises.tests:
p1 = {"A": [], "B": ["A"], "C": ["B"], "D": ["B"], "E": ["D"], "F": ["C", "E"], "G": ["E"]}
assert merge_base(p1, "F", "G") == "E", merge_base(p1, "F", "G")
assert merge_base(p1, "C", "E") == "B"
assert merge_base(p1, "C", "C") == "C"
assert merge_base(p1, "B", "G") == "B"           # an ancestor of the other: a fast-forward
p2 = {"r": [], "x1": ["r"], "x2": ["x1"], "y1": ["r"], "y2": ["y1"], "m": ["x2", "y2"], "x3": ["x2"], "z": ["m"]}
assert merge_base(p2, "x3", "z") == "x2", merge_base(p2, "x3", "z")
assert merge_base(p2, "y2", "x3") == "r"
chain = {str(i): ([str(i - 1)] if i else []) for i in range(2000)}
chain["side"] = ["1000"]
assert merge_base(chain, "1999", "side") == "1000"
hints: First compute all ancestors of a commit with a graph search (iterative, to avoid deep recursion on long histories).
The common ancestors are the intersection of the two ancestor sets.
A common ancestor is not "best" if it is a proper ancestor of another common ancestor. Collect all proper ancestors of all common ancestors and subtract them.

exercises.tests:
base = {"a.txt": "1", "b.txt": "1"}
ours = {"a.txt": "2", "b.txt": "1"}
theirs = {"a.txt": "1", "b.txt": "3", "c.txt": "new"}
assert merge3(base, ours, theirs) == ({"a.txt": "2", "b.txt": "3", "c.txt": "new"}, [])

# deletion on one side, untouched on the other: the file is deleted
assert merge3({"old.py": "x", "k": "1"}, {"k": "1"}, {"old.py": "x", "k": "1"}) == ({"k": "1"}, [])
assert merge3({"old.py": "x"}, {"old.py": "x"}, {}) == ({}, [])
# identical changes on both sides are not a conflict
assert merge3({"f": "1"}, {"f": "2"}, {"f": "2"}) == ({"f": "2"}, [])
# both changed differently: conflict, keep ours
assert merge3({"f": "1", "g": "1"}, {"f": "2", "g": "1"}, {"f": "3", "g": "1"}) == ({"f": "2", "g": "1"}, ["f"])
# we deleted, they modified: conflict, and our deletion stays
assert merge3({"f": "1"}, {}, {"f": "2"}) == ({}, ["f"])
# both added the same path with different contents: conflict
assert merge3({}, {"n": "ours"}, {"n": "theirs"}) == ({"n": "ours"}, ["n"])
# conflicts come back sorted
m, c = merge3({"z": "0", "a": "0"}, {"z": "1", "a": "1"}, {"z": "2", "a": "2"})
assert c == ["a", "z"], c
hints: Loop over every path that appears in *any* of the three snapshots, and use `dict.get`, which returns `None` for a missing path, so that "deleted" and "absent" are just the value `None`.
Check the cases in order: `o == t`, then `o == b`, then `t == b`, else conflict.
Only store a path in `merged` if the chosen result is not `None`.

exercises.prompt: You created `feature` from `main` and made three commits on it. Nobody has committed to `main` since. What happens when you run `git switch main` and then `git merge feature`?

options.label: A fast-forward: the `main` ref moves to `feature`'s latest commit, and no new commit is created.
options.feedback: Yes. `main`'s commit is an ancestor of `feature`'s tip, so there is nothing to combine; moving the pointer gives exactly the merged state.

options.label: Git creates a merge commit with two parents, because a merge always creates one.
options.feedback: Not yet — by default Git fast-forwards when it can. (Some teams pass `--no-ff` to force a merge commit, to record that a branch existed.)

options.label: Git copies the three commits onto `main`, giving them new hashes.
options.feedback: Not yet — that describes rebasing or cherry-picking. A fast-forward reuses the very same commit objects.

options.label: Git reports a conflict, because `main` and `feature` have different trees.
options.feedback: Not yet — conflicts arise only when *both* sides changed the same thing since the merge base. Here only `feature` changed anything.

hints: What is the merge base of `main` and `feature` here?
exercises.solution: The merge base of `main` and `feature` is `main`'s current commit itself, since `feature` grew from it. Every change on `feature` is new and nothing on `main` needs reconciling, so Git simply moves the `main` ref forward to `feature`'s tip: a **fast-forward**. No objects are created and the hashes do not change. Teams that want every feature visible as a unit in the history use `git merge --no-ff` to create a merge commit anyway; teams that prefer a linear history allow or require fast-forwards.

exercises.prompt: Which commit message best follows the conventions in the lesson?

options.label: `Fixed some bugs in the export code and also cleaned things up a bit while I was there`
options.feedback: Not yet — it is too long for a summary line, mixes two unrelated changes (which should be two commits), and does not say which bug or why.

options.label: `Escape commas in CSV export` + blank line + a body: `Station names such as "Cusco, Peru" split into two columns, so imports into spreadsheets shifted every later field. Quote any field that contains a comma or quote, per RFC 4180. Fixes #212.`
options.feedback: Yes: a short imperative summary, then a body explaining the symptom, the cause and the fix, and a link to the issue.

options.label: `wip`
options.feedback: Not yet — fine on a private branch you will tidy up before review, but on a shared branch it tells future readers nothing.

options.label: `Changed export.py line 88 from split(',') to csv.reader`
options.feedback: Not yet — the diff already shows *what* changed on which line. The message should explain *why*.

hints: A good summary line completes the sentence "If applied, this commit will …".
Which message would help someone running `git blame` on the export code a year from now?
exercises.solution: Option (b) has every element: a summary under about 50 characters in the imperative mood, a blank line, and a body that explains the *symptom* (shifted columns), the *cause* (unquoted commas) and the *decision* (quote per the CSV standard), ending with the issue reference. Option (a) bundles unrelated changes, (c) is a placeholder, and (d) restates the diff. A useful test: could someone decide whether it is safe to revert this commit from the message alone?

exercises.prompt: You are reviewing a pull request that adds retry logic to a function uploading sensor readings. You notice the loop retries forever if the server keeps failing. Which comment is most effective?

options.label: "This is wrong. Never write infinite loops."
options.feedback: Not yet — it is about a real problem, but it neither explains the consequence nor suggests a fix, and its tone invites defensiveness rather than a better patch.

options.label: "If the server is down for a long time, this loop never exits, and the upload worker stops processing other stations. Could we cap the attempts (say 5, with backoff) and then surface the error? Happy to pair on it."
options.feedback: Yes: it names the concrete failure scenario and its consequence, proposes a direction, and leaves room for the author's judgement.

options.label: Approve it without comment: the author is senior and probably considered it.
options.feedback: Not yet — review exists precisely so that a second person checks. Raising a real correctness risk is the reviewer's job, whoever the author is.

options.label: "nit: I would call this variable `attempt` instead of `i`."
options.feedback: Not yet — a fine suggestion on its own, but leaving only a naming nit while an infinite-loop bug goes unmentioned gets the priorities backwards.

hints: Good review comments explain the consequence, not just the rule.
Which comment would you most like to receive on your own code?
exercises.solution: Comment (b) does what an effective review comment should: it describes the **scenario** (the server is down for a long time), the **consequence** (the worker stalls for every station), and a **suggested direction** (cap attempts, back off, surface the error), phrased as a question that respects the author's knowledge of the code. Correctness problems come before naming nits, and seniority is not a reason to skip them. Retries, backoff and why unbounded retries are dangerous are covered in detail in the distributed systems lesson.
